answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Seneca. The line closes a thought in his ‘Moral Letters to Lucilius’, Letter 71 (“On the Supreme Good”), §3: “Our plans miscarry because they have no aim.” This exact English is Richard M. Gummere’s 1920 Loeb translation of the Latin “Ignoranti quem portum petat, nullus suus ventus est.”

source.excerpt: Our plans miscarry because they have no aim. When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the maxim to Seneca and prints the Latin original, “Ignoranti quem portum petat, nullus suus ventus est” — see Quote Investigator’s investigation.
The exact English wording appears in Letter 71, §3, right after “Our plans miscarry because they have no aim” — confirmed on Wikisource’s text of Letter 71.
That English is Richard M. Gummere’s translation for the Loeb Classical Library edition (Vol. II, 1920).
source.excerptNote: Gummere’s 1920 Loeb rendering of Letter 71, §3. The two sentences run together in Seneca’s text; the harbour line is the punchline of the first.

source.rightsNote: Seneca’s Latin has been in the public domain for two millennia. The precise English wording shown here is Richard M. Gummere’s translation, first published in the Loeb Classical Library in 1920 — before 1931, so it is public domain in the United States. A different modern translation of the same passage could still be in copyright.

author.name: Seneca the Younger
author.heading: About Seneca the Younger
author.metaLine: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist & statesman
author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca, called “the Younger,” was a Roman Stoic philosopher, playwright, and adviser to the emperor Nero. His Epistulae Morales ad Lucilius — 124 letters on ethics and the good life — are among the most-quoted works of ancient Stoicism. Forced by Nero to take his own life in AD 65, he is one of antiquity’s most cited (and most misquoted) moralists.

misattribution.heading: Wait — isn't this Oscar Wilde?
misattribution.intro: The line is authentically Seneca’s, but it circulates under the wrong name and in reworded forms that Seneca never wrote.

items.why: The saying circulates — especially in German, as “Günstige Winde kann nur der nutzen, der weiß, wohin er will” — credited to Wilde. Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence linking it to Wilde, who “attracts a large number of spurious attributions.”

Popular forms such as “If one does not know to which port one is sailing, no wind is favourable” (the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations wording) and “If a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is favourable” (an 1881 Latin schoolbook) are later reworkings of the same Latin, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the words are Seneca’s, from Letter 71 of the Moral Letters to Lucilius; this exact English is Gummere’s 1920 translation of “Ignoranti quem portum petat, nullus suus ventus est” — see Wikisource.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Seneca’s point in Letter 71 is not about sailing at all: it is that a life without a settled aim cannot judge what helps or hinders it. If you don’t know your destination, no circumstance is ‘favourable,’ because you have no standard by which to call it so.
detailsBody: The maxim caps the sentence “Our plans miscarry because they have no aim,” part of Seneca’s larger claim in Letter 71 that the supreme good — virtue — is the one fixed harbour that gives every other choice its direction.
